frame: Object pronoun, split, matched: singular subject 'a diner' and verb; the singular antecedent 'price' is the object of the opening participial phrase; nearer singular nouns 'menu card' and 'study' stand between it and the pronoun; plural 'prices' gives 'them' a referent, which only the later comparison 'than the rounded prices' rules out
deletion_test: Delete the opening phrase and the sentence names no singular thing a diner could judge 'more carefully set than the rounded prices'; 'it' loses its antecedent and the pronoun's number is no longer settled.

distractor_pulls.judges them: Right verb; 'several rounded prices' is the nearest plural and the passage is about prices in general, so a student who stops before 'than the rounded prices' takes 'them'.
distractor_pulls.judge them: A reader who carries the plural topic 'prices' forward and treats 'a diner in such a study' as a generic statement about diners makes both halves plural.
distractor_pulls.judge it: Finds the one precise price correctly but reads 'a diner in such a study typically' as a statement about diners in general and makes the verb plural.

distractor_kills.judges them: Pronoun-antecedent agreement and logical comparison: the only plural antecedent is 'rounded prices', and 'judges them more carefully set by the restaurant than the rounded prices' compares those prices with themselves.
distractor_kills.judge them: Subject-verb agreement: 'a diner' is singular; the pronoun also fails as above.
distractor_kills.judge it: Subject-verb agreement: 'a diner' is singular and needs 'judges'.

frame: Simple past keyed against 'has been + widespread': singular subject 'Bilingualism' is the first noun and the noun before the blank; plural 'vendors' 4 words after; the time phrase 'at the height of the harbor's grain trade' 9 words after names a period that the next sentence ('That trade collapsed') shows is finished; the preceding sentence is in the present perfect
decider_quote: at the height of the harbor's grain trade
deletion_test: 'Bilingualism ___ widespread among the market vendors of the old quarter', after a sentence in the present perfect, accepts both 'has been widespread' and 'was widespread'.

distractor_pulls.has been widespread: The preceding sentence is in the present perfect ('have argued', 'has shaped'), and 'at the height of' does not by itself say the trade is over; a student who does not read on to 'That trade collapsed' keeps the perfect.
distractor_pulls.were widespread: Right tense; 'the market vendors' sits right after the blank and names the people who were bilingual, so the verb is made plural.
distractor_pulls.have been widespread: Combines the plural pull of 'vendors' with the present-perfect frame of the first sentence.

distractor_kills.has been widespread: Verb aspect: the present perfect cannot be tied to a finished past period, and the next sentence makes 'the height of the harbor's grain trade' finished ('That trade collapsed').
distractor_kills.were widespread: Subject-verb agreement: the subject is 'Bilingualism', singular; 'vendors' is the object of 'among'.

hostile_reader.options_only_pick: 'was widespread' is shortest by one letter; no extra word

frame: Sentence-final nonrestrictive appositive 'the Sentinel, whose ...' after 'the town's newspaper'; the FOLLOWING sentence implies, without a count, that the town had only one paper
structure: independent clause ending 'rely heavily on the town's newspaper' + appositive noun phrase 'the Sentinel' with a relative clause running to the end of the sentence
decider_quote: The valley had no other printing press in those years

distractor_pulls.newspaper the: Reads like 'the novelist Sato': a role noun followed directly by a name is a familiar restrictive pattern, and nothing before the blank says how many papers the town had.
distractor_pulls.newspaper; the: The words after the blank contain finite verbs ('attended', 'printed'), so a reader who does not notice 'whose' takes 'the Sentinel ... attended' as a second independent clause.
distractor_pulls.newspaper the,: A reader who wants the name set off but hears the pause after 'the' places the comma there (the row's required one-word-off comma; the one allowed glance strike).

distractor_kills.newspaper the: Restrictive versus nonrestrictive: with no other press in the valley and the rival paper printed elsewhere, the town had one newspaper, so the name adds information and must be set off.
distractor_kills.newspaper; the: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; 'the Sentinel, whose two reporters ...' has no main verb of its own.
distractor_kills.newspaper the,: A comma cannot separate a determiner from the noun it introduces.

hostile_reader.options_only_pick: the shifted comma is strikable at a glance (row-mandated, the one allowed)
hostile_reader.changed: REVISED: removed the first-sentence count 'exactly one newspaper'; the only-one fact now comes AFTER the blank and must be inferred ('no other printing press', the competing paper came from forty miles away)

frame: No number trap before the blank: plural 'tenants' is the first noun; the interrupting reporting clause 'the interviewers found' (plural noun, past verb) sits before the blank; singular 'increase' after the blank; 'are V-ing'; present 'as long as' conditional 8 words after
decider_quote: as long as that increase stays below the ceiling
deletion_test: 'Long-term tenants, the interviewers found, ___ the building's yearly increase without formal complaint' accepts 'were accepting' (backshifted after 'found') and 'are accepting' alike.

distractor_pulls.were accepting: The reporting verb right before the blank is past ('the interviewers found'), and reported findings are normally backshifted; the first sentence narrates finished fieldwork too.
distractor_pulls.is accepting: The singular 'increase' after the blank is what the clause is about, and 'the building's yearly increase' reads as the topic.
distractor_pulls.was accepting: Backshift after 'found' plus the singular nouns after the blank.

distractor_kills.were accepting: Verb tense: the conditional 'as long as that increase stays' is present, and the main clause it conditions must match it; 'were accepting ... as long as that increase stays' mixes tenses.
distractor_kills.is accepting: Subject-verb agreement: the subject is 'Long-term tenants', plural.

hostile_reader.changed: REVISED: the subject no longer sits directly before the blank (an interrupting past reporting clause does), which also makes backshifted 'were accepting' a real pull; dropped the second present verb 'publishes'. The number half remains easy by the row's design (Pos after, no trap before the blank)

frame: Perfect progressive keyed: singular head 'study' between the plural determiner 'Their' and 'of unpaid interns and paid classmates' (ending plural); since-phrase 'since that first recruitment drive' 7 words after the blank; the preceding sentence narrates the study's start in the past
deletion_test: 'Their study of unpaid interns and paid classmates ___ both groups through the job market', after a past-tense sentence, accepts both 'has been following' and 'was following'.

distractor_pulls.was following: The first sentence narrates the study's launch in the past ('began recruiting', 'crashed'), and 'that first recruitment drive' points back to that past event, so a student with the right number continues the narrative.
distractor_pulls.have been following: Right aspect; the subject opens with the plural 'Their' and ends on a compound of two plurals, so the whole subject sounds plural.
distractor_pulls.were following: The plural cues of the subject plus the past narrative.

distractor_kills.was following: Verb aspect: a 'since' phrase naming a starting point requires a perfect form.
distractor_kills.have been following: Subject-verb agreement: the head is 'study', singular; 'Their' is a determiner and 'interns and paid classmates' is the object of 'of'.

heuristics_that_give_key: (a) opposite of the noun before the blank

frame: Singular head 'suffix' + 'on verbs' ending plural; blank is auxiliary + 'never'; the phrase 'under pressure from the national schools' completes 'is never under pressure' as a clause until the intransitive participle 'disappeared' arrives and settles have over be
deletion_test: Delete 'fully disappeared' and 'The polite suffix on verbs ___ under pressure from the national schools' takes 'is never' (be + prepositional complement) and leaves 'has never' without a participle: the auxiliary can no longer be chosen.

distractor_pulls.is never: Right number; 'is never under pressure from the national schools' is a complete, idiomatic be-clause, so a reader who stops at 'schools' has a finished sentence.
distractor_pulls.have never: Right auxiliary; 'verbs' sits right before the blank.
distractor_pulls.are never: The adjacent plural 'verbs' plus the complete-looking 'are never under pressure' clause.

distractor_kills.is never: Verb form: 'disappeared' is the past participle of an intransitive verb; it cannot follow 'be' as a passive or as a predicate adjective, so the perfect auxiliary is required.
distractor_kills.have never: Subject-verb agreement: the head is 'suffix', singular.

heuristics_that_give_key: (a) opposite of the noun before the blank

frame: Possessive split, mismatched: the blank's sentence opens with plural 'Field teams'; the singular owner 'questionnaire' is named early in the relative clause 'that carry the statistics office's questionnaire into remote hill villages in the north'; between owner and blank stand plural 'villages' and singular 'north' (neither the owner); then 'have translated its'
deletion_test: Delete 'the statistics office's questionnaire' (leaving 'Field teams that carry ... into remote hill villages in the north') and no document whose wording is translated is named in the sentence; 'its' could reach only 'north' and 'their' the villages or teams, so the possessive is no longer decided.

distractor_pulls.have translated their: Right verb; the nearest plural, 'remote hill villages', and the teams themselves both sit closer to the blank than the questionnaire, and copying the verb's number onto the possessive feels consistent.
distractor_pulls.has translated its: Right possessive; the long relative clause ends on 'in the north', so a reader who loses the head 'teams' makes the verb singular.
distractor_pulls.has translated their: Takes the adjacent 'north' for the verb and the nearest plural, 'villages', for the owner, the two nearest nouns of each number.

distractor_kills.have translated their: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: the wording is that of 'the statistics office's questionnaire' (singular); the villages and the teams own no wording ('drafted in the capital'), and the provinces' local forms were replaced.
distractor_kills.has translated its: Subject-verb agreement: the subject is 'Field teams', plural; 'north' ends the relative clause.

frame: Active present perfect keyed: plural head 'volunteers' + postposed adjective phrase 'responsible for the branch's homework desk' ending singular, after the opening adjective phrase 'Dependent on a single municipal grant'; the since-phrase arrives 16 words after the blank, past an appositive about former pupils of a shuttered school
deletion_test: 'the volunteers responsible for the branch's homework desk ___ about forty students a week, most of them former pupils of the shuttered middle school' accepts both 'have coached' and 'were coaching'.

distractor_pulls.were coaching: Right number; the words after the blank are about a closed past ('former pupils', 'shuttered middle school'), and 'a week' describes a routine, which the past progressive expresses; the 'since' phrase is sixteen words away.
distractor_pulls.has coached: Right aspect; 'desk' ends the subject, 'branch's' and 'grant' are singular too, so the subject seems singular.
distractor_pulls.was coaching: The singular nouns around the subject plus the past-time words after the blank.

distractor_kills.were coaching: Verb aspect: a 'since' phrase naming a starting point requires a perfect form.
distractor_kills.has coached: Subject-verb agreement: the subject is 'volunteers', plural; 'desk' is the object of 'for' inside the adjective phrase.

frame: Independent clause ending 'a bookkeeper named Ursula Wexler' + noun phrase 'the widow of the shop's first foreman' followed by 'trained in double-entry accounts', which reads as the finite verb of a second clause until 'by her own father' shows it is a passive participle; no comma is printed after the noun phrase
structure: left: complete clause 'Its entries were made by a bookkeeper named Ursula Wexler'; right: noun phrase 'the widow of the shop's first foreman' + participial modifier 'trained in double-entry accounts by her own father', no finite verb before the period

distractor_pulls.Wexler; the: 'the widow of the shop's first foreman trained in double-entry accounts' is a complete clause on a first reading (active 'trained in', as in 'she trained in law'), so a semicolon between two clauses about the bookkeeper looks right; only 'by her own father' undoes it.
distractor_pulls.Wexler: the: Under the same clause reading, the second part explains who the bookkeeper was, and colons introduce explanations.
distractor_pulls.Wexler the: Reads 'the widow of the shop's first foreman' as part of a name-plus-title unit (like 'Catherine the Great'), so no mark seems needed; no closing comma is printed to signal an inserted phrase.

distractor_kills.Wexler; the: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause; 'trained ... by her own father' is a passive participle without a helping verb, so the words after the blank have no finite verb.
distractor_kills.Wexler: the: The clause before the blank is complete and points ahead to nothing; a nonessential description of a fully named person is set off with a comma.
distractor_kills.Wexler the: A nonrestrictive appositive after a proper name must be set off; running it on makes the description read as part of the name.

frame: Plain singular keyed: 'the parliamentarian rules on each procedural objection'; 'rules' reads naturally as a noun after a possessive ('the parliamentarian's rules'); the only other verb in the clause is inside 'before debate resumes'; the FOLLOWING sentence fixes one holder ('that duty' ... 'a lone appointee')
structure: 'the ___' is the subject of the verb 'rules'; the possessive reading makes 'rules on each procedural objection' a verbless noun phrase; the last sentence says the duty belongs to a lone appointee
decider_quote: The city charter assigns that duty to a lone appointee

distractor_pulls.parliamentarian's: 'the parliamentarian's rules' is a familiar phrase (rules of order are what a parliamentarian keeps), and 'resumes' supplies a verb later in the sentence, so a reader who does not parse the before-clause accepts the possessive.
distractor_pulls.parliamentarians: A reader who has not reached the last sentence assumes a council has several procedural officers, and 'the parliamentarians rules' passes a quick ear test when 'rules' is half-read as a noun.
distractor_pulls.parliamentarians': Combines the possessive reading of 'rules' with the expectation that a council has several officers.

distractor_kills.parliamentarian's: Possessive misuse: 'rules' must be the main verb of the first clause ('resumes' belongs to the subordinate 'before' clause); a possessive makes it a noun and leaves the clause without a verb.
distractor_kills.parliamentarians: Number and agreement: one appointee holds the duty (last sentence), and the singular verb 'rules' needs a singular subject.
distractor_kills.parliamentarians': Both errors: no main verb, and a plural owner where there is one appointee.
